Fir
fẽr
n. (an evergreen timber tree; rendering Hebrew berosh)
Old Norse fyri. The fir is Scripture's second timber after cedar — a building wood and a promise of restoration.

Biblical Definition

Fir is an evergreen timber. Solomon's temple used it for floors and doors (1Ki 6:15,34), and the ships of Tyre were made of it (Eze 27:5). Isaiah makes it a sign of reversal: “Instead of the thorn shall come up the fir tree, and instead of the brier shall come up the myrtle tree: and it shall be to the LORD for a name, for an everlasting sign that shall not be cut off” (Isa 55:13). The trees rejoice at Babylon's fall (Isa 14:8).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines fir as a tree of the genus Pinus, of several species, valued for its timber and for turpentine.

expand to see more

FIR, n. A tree of the genus Pinus, from which the resinous substance called turpentine is obtained; the timber is valuable for building.

Key Scripture

Isa 55:13 — "Instead of the thorn shall come up the fir tree, and instead of the brier shall come up the myrtle tree: and it shall be to the LORD for a name, for an everlasting sign that shall not be cut off."

1Ki 6:15 — "And he built the walls of the house within with boards of cedar, both the floor of the house, and the walls of the cieling: and he covered them on the inside with wood, and covered the floor of the house with planks of fir."

Isa 14:8 — "Yea, the fir trees rejoice at thee, and the cedars of Lebanon, saying, Since thou art laid down, no feller is come up against us."

Hos 14:8 — "Ephraim shall say, What have I to do any more with idols? I have heard him, and observed him: I am like a green fir tree. From me is thy fruit found."

Modern Corruption

Restoration is imagined as removing what is bad, and Isaiah promises a substitution — the thorn does not merely go, a fir comes up in its place.

expand to see more

Isaiah 55 ends with an exchange rather than a clearance. Instead of the thorn shall come up the fir tree, and instead of the brier shall come up the myrtle tree. Thorns entered the world with the curse in Genesis 3, so their replacement by timber and fragrance is a reversal of that sentence, and the verse says it shall be to the LORD for a name, an everlasting sign that shall not be cut off. The new growth is itself the monument.

The chapter's placement matters. This follows the great invitation — ho, every one that thirsteth — and the promise that God's word shall not return void. The thorn-for-fir exchange is what the word accomplishes when it goes out, which makes it a description of what preaching does in a life rather than merely a picture of the world to come.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew berosh (H1265), fir or cypress — a timber tree of Lebanon, paired constantly with cedar.

expand to see more

Hebrew berosh (H1265) — fir, cypress; Isaiah 55:13, 1 Kings 5:8, 6:15, Ezekiel 27:5.

Hebrew hadas (H1918) — myrtle; the companion tree in Isaiah 55:13.

Usage

"“Instead of the thorn shall come up the fir tree” — substitution, not clearance."

"“An everlasting sign that shall not be cut off” — the growth is the monument."

"“The fir trees rejoice at thee” — the forest glad at a tyrant's fall."
